title.en: AP Statistics Exam Format & Study Design

body.en: AP Statistics introduces students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. The course follows four interconnected curriculum pillars: Exploring Data (20–30%), Sampling and Experimentation (12–15%), Probability and Distributions (20–30%), and Statistical Inference (30–40%).

label.en: ● The 4 AP Statistics Course Skills & Mathematical Practices

body.en:
Every exam question assesses one or more of the four College Board Course Skills:

SkillTitleCore Competency & Assessment Focus
Skill 1Selecting Statistical MethodsSelect an appropriate method for collecting data, choose between observational studies vs experiments, and specify appropriate inference procedures (e.g. 1-prop z, 2-sample t, chi-square).
Skill 2Data AnalysisConstruct and interpret graphical displays (histograms, boxplots, scatterplots) and calculate numerical summaries (mean, median, standard deviation, IQR, z-scores).
Skill 3Exploring Random PatternsApply probability rules, calculate expected values and standard deviations of random variables, and determine probabilities from normal, binomial, and geometric models.
Skill 4Statistical ArgumentationConstruct and interpret confidence intervals, perform significance tests, check all necessary conditions, and state conclusions strictly in context without 'accepting' null hypotheses.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (AP Statistics Exam Format & Study Design)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

A student allocates 90 minutes to complete the 40 multiple-choice questions in Section I. What is the average time available per question in minutes and seconds?

Divide total time by number of questions: \[ \frac{90\text{ minutes}}{40\text{ questions}} = 2.25\text{ minutes}. \] Convert the decimal fraction of a minute to seconds: \[ 0.25 \times 60 = 15\text{ seconds} \implies \mathbf{2\text{ minutes and }15\text{ seconds per question}}. \]

label.en: Worked Example \(B\) — AP Statistics Exam Format & Study Design (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): In a two-stage probability tree for events \( U \) and \( V \), \( P(U) = 0.3 \) and \( P(V \mid U) = 0.6 \). What is the expected frequency \( r = 100 \cdot P(U \cap V) \) in \( 100 \) independent trials?

Step-by-Step Solution: Since \( P(U \cap V) = 0.3 \times 0.6 = 0.18 \), the expected count in 100 trials is \( 18 \).

rows.en: The \(25\%\) reduction applies to the larger base \(1.25 Q_0\), not \(Q_0\).
Dividing by a negative number reverses order on the real number line.
Flip the inequality symbol whenever multiplying or dividing by a negative: \(x < -4\).
Computing round-trip average speed as \(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\)
Time spent at the slower speed is longer than time spent at the faster speed.
Use total distance over total time: \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

Section II of the AP Statistics exam has 90 minutes allocated for 6 Free-Response Questions. If a student reserves 25 minutes for Question 6 (the Investigative Task), what is the exact average time available per question for Questions 1 through 5?

solution.en:
Calculate the remaining time for Questions 1 through 5: \[ 90 - 25 = 65\text{ minutes}. \]

Divide by 5 questions: \[ \frac{65\text{ minutes}}{5\text{ questions}} = \mathbf{13\text{ minutes per question}}. \]

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Investigative Task Strategy & Calculator Functions

body.en: Master specialized calculator commands (normalcdf, invNorm, tcdf, 1-PropZTest) and learn how to tackle novel statistical reasoning in Question 6.

caption.en: AP Statistics exam score weighting across the curriculum units.

label.en: ● Standard Graphing Calculator Syntax & Notation Requirements

body.en:
On AP Free-Response Questions, writing only calculator syntax (like normalcdf(...)) without labeling inputs yields only partial credit. You must either write the standard algebraic formula OR clearly label each input parameter:

  • Normal Distribution: normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ) and invNorm(area to left, μ, σ). Always specify the standardized boundary: \[ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}. \]
  • Student's t Distribution: tcdf(lower, upper, df) and invT(area to left, df). Always state degrees of freedom \(df = n - 1\).
  • Binomial Distribution: binompdf(n, p, k) for \(P(X = k)\) and binomcdf(n, p, k) for \(P(X \le k)\). Specify \(n\), \(p\), and \(k\).
  • Inference Tests: 1-PropZTest, 2-PropZTest, 2-SampleTTest, and LinRegTTest. Always explicitly state the name of the test, test statistic \(z\) or \(t\), degrees of freedom, and p-value.

label.en: ⏱ Free Response Strategy & Question 6 Investigative Task

body.en:
• Pacing: Allot 65 minutes for Questions 1–5 (~13 minutes each) and reserve a full 25 minutes for Question 6 (the Investigative Task). Question 6 is worth 25% of your total FRQ section score (12.5% of total exam score)!
  • Calculator & Formula Sheet: You are provided the official College Board formula sheet and statistical tables. Graphing calculators are permitted throughout the entire exam.
  • Show Statistical Notation: When writing calculator commands, always write the standard mathematical formula or label your inputs (e.g., lower, upper, mean, SD) to receive full credit.
  • Question 6 Strategy: Question 6 introduces a novel scenario, formula, or non-standard distribution not explicitly in the course description. Read the prompts carefully: each part builds sequentially on the previous part!

A student needs to find the probability that a standard normal variable \(Z\) exceeds 1.75. Write the calculator syntax with labeled inputs and evaluate the probability to four decimal places.

Lower bound = 1.75, Upper bound = \(10^{99}\) (or \(\infty\)), Mean \(\mu = 0\), Standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\): \[ P(Z > 1.75) = \text{normalcdf}(\text{lower} = 1.75, \text{upper} = 10^{99}, \mu = 0, \sigma = 1) \approx \mathbf{0.0401}. \]

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Find the critical value \(z^*\) required to construct a 98% confidence interval for a population proportion, rounded to three decimal places.

solution.en:
For a 98% confidence interval, the central area is 0.98, leaving 0.02 split equally between both tails (0.01 in each tail). The area to the left of the upper critical value is: \[ 1 - 0.01 = 0.99. \]

Using the inverse normal function: \[ z^* = \text{invNorm}(\text{area} = 0.99, \mu = 0, \sigma = 1) \approx \mathbf{2.326}. \]

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in AP Statistics Exam Format & Study Design and start from \(z^*\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( 1 - 0.01 = 0.99. \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — FRQ Scoring Rules, Holistic Rubrics & Composite Scores

body.en: Apply College Board rubric standards: E/P/I scoring conversions, context in conclusions, comparative language, avoiding 'accepting H0', checking inference conditions, and analyzing Type I vs Type II errors.

label.en: ● College Board Holistic Scoring \((E/P/I)\) & Composite Calculation

body.en:
Each FRQ part is scored as E (Essentially Correct), P (Partially Correct), or I (Incorrect):

  • Question Score (0–4 Scale): A question with three parts (a, b, c) scores: 4 = EEE; 3 = EEP; 2 = EPP or EEI; 1 = PPI or EII; 0 = III or PII.
  • Section II Composite Conversion: Questions 1–5 raw scores are each multiplied by 1.875 (max 7.5 points each, totaling 37.5 points). Question 6 raw score is multiplied by 3.125 (max 12.5 points).
  • Total Composite Score: Section I (40 MCQ × 1.25 = 50 max) + Section II (50 max) = 100 composite points. Typically, ~70+ points earns a score of 5, ~58–69 earns a 4, and ~45–57 earns a 3.

label.en: ▲ The 4 Golden Rules of AP Statistics FRQs

body.en:
• 1. Always Interpret in Context: Every definition, slope, intercept, confidence interval, or conclusion MUST include the specific context (variable names, population, units). An answer with perfect numbers but missing context receives only Partial credit.
  • 2. Use Comparative Language: When comparing two distributions, never just list values for each separately. You must explicitly use comparative words: 'The median salary of Group A is greater than the median salary of Group B.'
  • 3. Never 'Accept' the Null Hypothesis: We never prove \(H_0\) is true; we only 'fail to reject \(H_0\)' due to insufficient evidence. Writing 'accept \(H_0\)' is an automatic deduction on AP rubrics.
  • 4. Check All Assumptions & Conditions: Never proceed to an inference calculation without explicitly naming and verifying the Random, 10% (independence), and Normality / Large Counts conditions.

A quality control test has \(H_0: p = 0.02\) vs \(H_a: p > 0.02\), where \(p\) is the proportion of defective microchips. Describe a Type I error, a Type II error, and state a consequence of each in context.

Type I Error: Rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true. Concluding that the defect rate is greater than 2% when it is actually at most 2%. Consequence: The company needlessly shuts down production or recalls good chips, wasting money.

Type II Error: Failing to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_a\) is true. Concluding that the defect rate is acceptable (\(\le 2%\)) when it is actually greater than 2%. Consequence: Defective microchips are shipped to customers, damaging the company's reputation.

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

An investigator conducts a hypothesis test at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\). Explain two distinct ways the investigator could increase the statistical power of the test without changing the true effect size.

solution.en:
1. Increase the sample size \(n\): A larger sample size reduces the standard error of the sample statistic (\(\sigma / \sqrt{n}\)), making the sampling distributions of \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) narrower, which increases the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis (power = \(1 - \beta\)).

2. Increase the significance level \(\alpha\) (e.g., from 0.05 to 0.10): A larger \(\alpha\) moves the critical rejection boundary closer to the center of \(H_0\), making it easier to reject \(H_0\) and thereby increasing power (at the expense of increasing the risk of a Type I error).

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(n\).
